title: Proposes Massive Offshore Drilling Expansion
description_short: Interior announced plans to open most U.S. coastal waters to offshore oil and gas leasing in a new proposed program.
description_medium: On January 4, 2018, the Interior Department announced a proposed program to make most U.S. coastal waters available for offshore oil and gas leasing. The plan concerned possible future lease sales, not immediate permission to drill. The supplied material does not identify which planning areas were included or excluded or when sales would occur.
description_long: The Interior Department’s January 2018 announcement proposed opening most U.S. coastal waters to oil and gas leasing. The headline attached to the linked report described the plan as covering about 90 percent of U.S. waters. The announcement concerned a proposed leasing program, under which areas could become available for future oil and gas bids; it did not mean that drilling began across those waters on January 4. The distinction is central to understanding the event: the department announced a plan for possible lease sales, while the specific regional schedule and later steps were not provided in the available account. The proposal signaled a broad expansion of federal offshore leasing, but the packet does not identify the included and excluded planning areas, the timing of sales or the environmental review sequence. Those details would be needed to describe where the policy might lead to exploration and what portions of the coast would be affected.

title: Ends FCC Broadband Privacy Rules
description_short: Trump signed legislation repealing FCC broadband privacy rules that limited ISPs from selling customers’ browsing data.
description_medium: On April 3, 2017, Donald Trump signed legislation repealing Federal Communications Commission broadband privacy rules. Those rules had restricted internet service providers from selling customers’ browsing data. The repeal removed that specific federal restriction on broadband providers’ use of customer information, shifting the privacy protections that applied to internet access services.
description_long: On April 3, 2017, President Donald Trump signed legislation repealing Federal Communications Commission rules for broadband privacy. The rules had limited internet service providers’ ability to sell customers’ browsing data. Broadband providers connect households to the internet and can observe information about how their service is used, so the rules addressed a different part of online privacy than settings on a particular website or app. The repeal removed that FCC restriction on how providers could use or sell customer browsing information. The event changed the federal regulatory framework for broadband data, even though the supplied account does not identify a specific provider sale or a particular customer whose data was disclosed. It was a policy change to the protection in place, rather than evidence that every provider immediately sold browsing histories. The legislation placed the future handling of this information in a less restrictive federal framework than the FCC rules that had been adopted for broadband customers.

title: U.S. Manufacturing Output Declines in 2019 Amid Trade-War Headwinds
description_short: U.S. Manufacturing Output Declines in 2019 Amid Trade-War Headwinds
description_medium: U.S. manufacturing output weakened in 2019 amid slower global growth and trade-policy uncertainty. Prior Federal Reserve and BLS research supports weaker output and tariff-related headwinds, but aggregate manufacturing employment over the year changed little rather than clearly declining. The entry should focus on output and trade-war effects rather than an unqualified annual jobs decline.
description_long: U.S. manufacturing output weakened in 2019 during a period of slower global growth and uncertainty over trade policy. The supplied correction says prior Federal Reserve and Bureau of Labor Statistics research found tariff-related headwinds, while aggregate manufacturing employment changed little over the year. These measures describe different parts of the economy: output tracks production, while employment counts workers. Weaker factory output therefore does not by itself establish a comparable drop in the number of manufacturing jobs. The episode was notable against the administration’s stated effort to use tariffs and an “America First” trade agenda to support domestic industry. The supplied material supports describing a difficult year for manufacturing production and a connection between tariffs and headwinds, but it gives no production percentage and does not isolate tariffs from slower global demand. It also does not support saying the sector lost jobs overall in 2019. The most accurate account is that output weakened amid trade-policy uncertainty, while annual employment was comparatively steady.

title: 200+ Federal Lawsuits Filed Against Trump Executive Orders Within First 90 Days
description_short: 200+ Federal Lawsuits Filed Against Trump Executive Orders Within First 90 Days
description_medium: A Reuters report published as Trump’s administration approached its 100-day mark counted more than 200 lawsuits challenging administration actions and more than 70 court rulings that blocked or delayed policies. The coverage spans a 100-day period, while this entry’s title specifies 90 days. Lawsuit counts describe challenges filed, not findings that every challenged action was unlawful.
description_long: By April 2025, more than 200 federal lawsuits had been filed across the country challenging Trump executive orders and agency actions taken in the first 90 days of his second term — an unprecedented volume of constitutional litigation reflecting the breadth and aggressiveness of the administration's unilateral executive actions. Plaintiffs included state attorneys general, civil liberties organizations, federal employee unions, universities, and private individuals. The lawsuits challenged actions including birthright citizenship restrictions, mass deportations, DOGE access to federal payment systems, funding freezes, DEI bans, and agency dismantlements. Courts had issued over 100 temporary restraining orders and preliminary injunctions blocking various actions. Legal scholars noted the litigation volume reflected both the administration's willingness to take legally dubious actions and the breadth of its ambitions to unilaterally reshape American governance. The administration responded by publicly attacking the judges issuing orders against it.
